name: Hair bangs / frame hairstyle for eyes

lead: Bangs (fringe in British usage) are hair that falls over the front hairline to cover the forehead, usually just above the eyebrows. In looksmaxxing discussions, bangs and face-framing styles are used to draw attention to the eyes and brow area and to change the apparent forehead and face shape. The change shows up as soon as the hair is cut.

Hair covering the forehead changes the visible hairline and frames the upper face; proponents say this shifts attention to the eyes and shortens a long forehead. Formal research is sparse; a 2022 cosmetology paper cited by Wikipedia paired five hairline shapes with fringe styles.

paras: People ask a stylist for a cut matched to their hairline and face shape, then style it day to day. Bangs need regular trimming to hold their shape, and they can be grown out if the look does not suit.
Styling carries no significant health risks. Bangs need regular trimming and styling, and the result depends on hair type and hairline.

angle.text: Bangs and face-framing hair draw attention to the eyes and brow area and change how the forehead and upper face look, a visible change from the haircut itself. Claims about eye emphasis have little formal research behind them.

lead: Bangs (called a fringe in British, Australian and New Zealand English) are strands of hair that fall over the forehead, usually just above the eyebrows. In looksmaxxing and styling discussions, bangs and other face-framing cuts are used to put the focus on the eyes and brows, shorten the look of a tall forehead, and soften or cover a receding hairline.[1][2][3][4]

The look is old and varied. Blunt, curtain, choppy, feathered and see-through fringes each frame the upper face differently, and Wikipedia records fringes in ancient Egypt, Greece and Rome, in medieval art, in Victorian fashion, in the Beatles-era 1960s and in a social-media revival of curtain bangs in the 2020s.[1] On looksmax.org a fringe is a recurring topic, with members trading cut and product advice for wavy and messy versions and pointing to male models such as Jordan Barrett as templates.[2][5][6]

Formal research on how fringes change the way eyes or faces are perceived is limited. A 2022 cosmetology paper by Park and Jang paired five hairline shapes with fringe styles using wig prototypes,[1] and experimental psychology work shows that hair and face are judged as a unit: a 2015 study found that hair can influence how attractive a face is rated even when it is not the thing being judged.[7]

paras: Wikipedia describes bangs as hair falling over the forehead, usually just above the eyebrows, with modern Western cuts typically straight but sometimes arced or left ragged.[1] The article lists blunt (straight-cut) bangs, the short frizzy Alexandra fringe, the mop-top, curtain bangs that part in the middle and frame the face, and choppy, heart, feather and see-through styles.[1]

Curtained hair is a related style with a long fringe parted in the middle or at the side. Wikipedia traces recurring versions from the early twentieth century, when working-class men in cities such as Glasgow, Manchester and Birmingham wore a longer undercut, through a late-1980s centre-parted style associated with new wave and synthpop fans, and a 2011 New York Times piece on the haircut's return, to current association with K-pop acts.[8]

The word "bangs" probably comes from "bang-off", hair cut straight across the front, which is related to "bang-tail", the practice of cutting horses' tails straight across, while "fringe" refers to the resemblance to decorative trim on items such as shawls.[1]

sections.h: How a fringe frames the eyes
paras: The forehead is bounded above by the hairline and below by the supraorbital ridge, and the eyebrows are not part of it.[9] A fringe sits on that boundary: hair just above or over the brows reduces the visible forehead area and creates a darker line directly above the eyes. Proponents describe the result as moving attention downward to the eyes and brows, and as shortening a forehead they consider tall.[2][3]

Eyebrows have a communicative role. A 2018 paper in Nature Ecology and Evolution, cited by Wikipedia, links humans' smooth foreheads and mobile eyebrows to the ability to express a wide range of subtle emotions.[10] Fringes that rest at or below brow level can partially cover that area, which is one reason stylists and forum members discuss length and thickness carefully; a T Nation reply to a member's photo suggested asking a hairdresser about a hairstyle that might offset the eyes and brow.[11]

Brow grooming is often discussed alongside the fringe: Wikipedia's eyebrow article lists tweezing, waxing, threading, trimming, tinting, pencils and gels, transplants and microblading as common methods.[10]

Fringes appear in ancient Egypt, Greece and Rome and in medieval art. European men kept wearing them in the Elizabethan era and Renaissance after they fell out of style for women, and in the 1600s clergy criticised them as vanity.[1]

Curled bangs returned for women in the Victorian era, and the Alexandra fringe, a mass of short frizzy bangs named after Alexandra of Denmark, was popular in the 1880s.[1] Wikipedia notes that in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries young immigrant women in the US wore bangs to cover blemishes such as smallpox scars and acne.[1]

Twentieth-century fringes included the Dutchboy bob, Mamie Eisenhower's short waved bangs and Audrey Hepburn's pixie cut. Bangs were uncommon on men until British bands led by the Beatles popularised the mop-top from about 1963, and Paul McCartney's 1964 mop-top is among the article's examples.[1] A thick blunt revival began in 2007, when Kate Moss got bangs in October of that year, and curtain bangs spread in the 2020s, largely through TikTok and videos of people cutting their own at home.[1]
The wider history of hairstyle includes a high forehead hairline being fashionable in the late fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, a contrast with later fringe periods.[12]

The 2022 study by Jin Hyun Park and Hyerroon Jang in the International Journal of Advanced Culture Technology identified five hairline shapes and paired each with a fringe: choppy bangs for round, heart bangs for heart, feather bangs for angular, blunt bangs for triangular and see-through bangs for flat. The authors built the pairings through wig prototypes and intend them as educational resources for cosmetology; Wikipedia reports that the study states hair accounts for over 70 percent of a person's perceived appearance.[1]

In experimental psychology, Saegusa, Intoy and Shimojo (2015, Frontiers in Psychology) proposed that face and hair share strong perceptual organisation and tested whether each influences the evaluation of the other. They found an asymmetry: task-irrelevant hair still influenced face attractiveness ratings, but only if the same rater had not already rated that hair, whereas the face affected hair ratings regardless.[7]

Mesko and Bereczkei (2004, Human Nature) tested six hairstyles on female faces against faces without visible hair and reported that long and medium-length hair raised attractiveness ratings and changed health ratings, while the other styles had no effect; the study concerned female faces and did not examine fringes specifically.[13]
No published study located has tested whether a fringe changes rated eye attractiveness or the apparent size of a forehead.

Threads on looksmax.org argue that a fringe suits almost everyone. One poster names male models he thinks look best in it, including Jordan Barrett, while others call it a way to cover a reduced hairline.[2][3][6] Wikipedia describes Barrett as an Australian model born in 1996 who has worked in campaigns for brands including Tom Ford, Balmain and Versace.[14] Members also trade product and cut advice for wavy and messy fringes, and there are threads titled "you must choose fringe or curtains", "wavy fringe mogs" and a Barrett fringe guide.[15][16][17]

Forum participants commonly discuss texture (straight, wavy, curly), the difference between a fringe and curtains, and the products used to hold a messy look. Social-media popularity is part of the conversation: one reply to the "fringe mogs" thread credits the look's spread to TikTok users.[2]

Posts that recommend a fringe for early recession tend to refer to Norwood stages. A thread titled "daily reminder if you have NW2 3 wear a fringe" ties the style to those stages.[4] The Hamilton-Norwood scale was introduced by anatomist James Hamilton in 1951 and revised by dermatologist O'Tar Norwood in 1975; stage 2 shows slight temple recession that some clinicians consider normal variation, while stage 3 is the earliest stage generally considered clinically significant, with deeper M- or V-shaped temple recession.[18]

Wikipedia's bangs article says fringes were historically worn to cover blemishes, and by construction they cover the forehead and upper hairline.[1] Wikipedia's Norwood article does not discuss hairstyling as a cover method, and no published study has tested how observers rate a fringed recessed hairline.[18]

In general terms, wearers describe a cut at the front that falls to or near the brows, shaped by a barber or stylist, and then styled with blow-drying and styling products to set direction and texture. Wavy or messy fringes are described as needing products or heat to hold shape, and one forum member described a stylist's messy fringe becoming harder to style once the cut changed his hair's behaviour.[5] Bangs need regular trimming to keep their length relative to the brows.[1]

No studies found on bangs and eye attractiveness. The nearest published work is the 2022 cosmetology paper pairing hairlines with fringe styles, and psychology studies of how hair influences face ratings.[1][7]
